Why Mussolini's ghost still haunts Italy

Why did Mussolini’s image survive long after the fall of fascism? Stephen Gundle explores Italy’s uneasy relationship with its dictator, from family photographs and fading fascist slogans to waxworks and modern popular culture

More than 80 years after Benito Mussolini’s death, his image still haunts Italy. Stephen Gundle speaks to Danny Bird about the dictator’s strange afterlife, and how Mussolini’s image survived in statues, 'ghost signs', films and even waxwork museums.

From his spectacular downfall in 1945 to the ways modern populists have inherited elements of his political style, Stephen questions what happens when a society doesn't fully confront its past – and why some dictators refuse to disappear.

item.title: Ask Ethan: What does it mean for atoms to “touch” each other?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: explains an idea clearly, useful vocabulary

One of the most counterintuitive things about existence is the notion of forces. In order to experience a force — that is, for one object to feel the influence of another object on it — two objects don’t necessarily even need to touch, or be in contact, with one another. Objects on Earth’s surface feel Earth’s gravity, but so do airplanes, satellites, and even the Moon: in the atmosphere, in low-Earth orbit, or even hundreds of thousands of kilometers away. An electrically charged object attracts and repels other electrical charges, regardless of how far away they are from each other. And, in a more familiar fashion, two magnets flipped so that their north poles face each other mutually repel one another so strongly that, for some magnets, even the strongest humans cannot bring them together into contact.

So what happens, then, when you try to bring your thumb and forefinger together? How close do they actually get, and do they ever truly “touch” one another? That’s what Peter Mead wants to know, writing in to ask:

“When I hold both hands out in front of me with my two forefingers pointed toward each other then bring them together, the space between my fingers gets smaller and smaller. I can see and hold them a bit less than a millimeter apart before they touch. Is there an instant, just before they touch, where my fingers are only an atom’s (or sub-atomic) width apart? Or does space somehow behave differently on such a small scale?”

Clearly, there’s a big range in between what we can see (a little under a millimeter) and the size of an atom (about one ten-billionth of a meter). Let’s find out what happens on those tiny scales.

Although we’re going to go down to very small scales to address this question in full, it’s important to recognize that “small” doesn’t necessarily mean “quantum” the way you might intuit. Yes, quantum effects typically rear their heads in isolated, single-or-few particle systems and tend to disappear if there are many particles interacting frequently, which is a hallmark of (most) macroscopic phenomena. However, while quantum effects normally appear on atomic scales or below, the more classical effects — including gravitational and electromagnetic effects — can never be ignored, and frequently dominate even over inherently quantum ones, even on the smallest scales of all.

Therefore, the first step is to recognize that your body is made of atoms, and that while the atoms within your fingers are bound together into molecules that comprise the organelles that make up your cells, it’s still fundamentally all atoms: electrons orbiting atomic nuclei. Even though it’s a long way down from the macroscopic world (fingers) to the atoms and the subatomic particles that make even the atoms up, that’s what the structure of matter truly looks like.

The atoms that are bound together — into molecules and then into larger structures — have restrictions on how their electrons can move. Even when shared between multiple atoms, the electrons orbit in cloud-like shells, and have a smeared-out distribution over time, dependent on what specific energy level (and molecular/atomic orbitals) they occupy. Whether you’re looking at a single atom or a larger structure made out of atoms, that’s the basic picture: there’s a negatively-charged electron cloud orbiting around a single or a series of multiple positively-charged atomic nucleus/nuclei.

Grateful for curious minds

So what happens, then, when you bring two atoms close to one another, as you might imagine happens when you bring your thumb and forefinger close to one another, but not so close as to have them touch?

It’s an interesting problem that most physics students learn how to solve in graduate school, where we all get the same answers if we perform our calculations correctly: the shape of the electron cloud that orbits around the atomic nucleus changes in response to the presence of the other nearby atom. Even though atoms (and molecules) themselves are neutral entities, the fact that they’re made of negatively and positively charged components allows them to do something extremely important: to polarize.

Polarization is a classical electromagnetic phenomenon, occurring wherever you have positive and negative charged together and the ability to have these charges move around and redistribute themselves relative to one another, dependent on the external forces acting on them. It turns out that while having a positive or negative charge nearby is an easy “external force” to visualize, simply bringing two uncharged but polarizable objects close to each other can, in fact, result in not only both objects polarizing, but in a net force being created between the two.

For example, let’s think about two simple atoms that are brought near to one another. Each one has a positively charged atomic nucleus and a diffuse cloud of negative charge around it. If you bring one into the vicinity of the other, they’ll initially remain spherical: with no net attractive or repulsive force. However, the closer you bring them together, the more the electron clouds will distort in their shape, creating a tiny dipole: where one positively charged nucleus is slightly off-center relative to the negatively-charged spherical distribution of the negative charges.…

item.title: 7 Cryptids Supposedly Roaming the Pacific Northwest
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Spend some time wandering through the forests of the Pacific Northwest, and youâll quickly understand why so many cryptids are said to have been spotted there. Those damp woods feel deeply alive and inherently magicalâor at least, that was my impression on a visit to Portlandâs Forest Park, a 5,200-acre, jewel-toned stretch of forest located right on the edge of the city.

With its whispering Douglas firs and thick layers of moss, the forest felt dense with wisdom and stories. Thanks to slips of sun poking through the cloud layer and sending shadows glancing off the trees, it was also quite easy to imagine flitting fairies or behemoths lurking out of the corner of my eye.

There are many well-documented, scientifically approved wonders within forests. The woods are full of medicinal plants, from anti-inflammatory mushrooms to vitamin-rich stinging nettle, and even simply spending time in the woods can improve mental and physical health. But of course, cryptids have long been rumored to haunt the woods along Americaâs northwestern edge.Â

SasquatchÂ

The most famous cryptid of them all just might be Sasquatch, also known as Bigfoot. This creature is typically described as an extremely hairy and tall humanoid creature, and sightings have been reported countless times over the years. Typically described as intelligent, shy, and wary of human contact, these creatures are sometimes said to be North Americaâs version of the Himalayan Yeti. In 1811, the explorer David Thompson discovered what he claimed were Sasquatch footprints, and sightings have continued near-ceaselessly since then.Â

Klicktitat Ape Cat

Also known as the Ebony Ape Cat, this panther-like mutant has reportedly been seen prowling the forests of the Pacific Northwest and the Columbia River Gorge. This jet-black cat looks like a panther but is said to stand up to five feet tall at the shoulder, and is also rumored to have primate-like facial features. Some legends claim that this creature escaped from a government lab linked to the Manhattan Project, and reports have mentioned battery drainage and electromagnetic interferenceâso if youâre hiking in the Pacific Northwest and your phone suddenly dies or your compass goes haywire, watch out.

Devilâs Lake Monster

This aquatic cryptid is said to come from Tillamook and Siletz legends, which tell of an ancient creature in the misty depths of Devilâs Lake near Lincoln City, Oregon that possesses many tentacles, a huge head, and glowing red eyes. Various stories describe multiple disappearances on the lake over the course of generations, and Native tribes in the area were said to make frequent offerings to appease the creature. There have also been whispers of occasional sightings in recent years.

Wallowa Lake Monster

This water-dwelling monster is said to live in Wallowa Lake, Oregon. It is sometimes said to resemble the long-necked plesiosaur, an ancient marine reptile that went extinct some 66 million years ago. This cryptid likely owes its existence to a Nez Perce legend about lovers from warring clans who were, the story goes, killed by it when they ventured out onto the lake one evening. An 1885 article in the Wallowa Chieftain described a localâs encounter with the creature, writing that it âseemed to have a large, flat head, something like that of a hippopotamus, and its neck, which was about ten feet in length, was as large around as a man's body.â

Gumberoo

This creature is said to resemble a black bear, but one thatâs completely hairless. Instead, this creature supposedly has leathery black skin as well as a furry beard and eyebrows. Stemming from lumberjack folklore of the 19th century, these beasts are rumored to be ravenously hungry and completely indestructible, though they can apparently be destroyed with fire.Â

Ball-Tailed Cat

Another creature from lumberjack folklore, this cat is said to resemble a panther, albeit with one key difference: it has a large club on its tail that the creature uses to kill its prey (and, one would assume, any unfortunate hikers who encounter it). Sometimes rumored to be red-eyed and endowed with sharp spikes on its tail, this creature is definitely not one youâd want to meet on the trail.

Tacoma Narrows Octopus

Said to live beneath the ruins of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Tacoma, Washington, this creature is rumored to weigh up to 600 pounds. Legends about this creature emerged after the bridge collapsed in 1940, a disaster that actually did create an artificial reef for numerous sea creaturesâincluding giant Pacific octopuses, which are real creatures that have tentacle-spans up to 20 feet. While stories of the so-called âKing Octopusâ may be pure legend, this cryptid has a more legitimate basis in reality than most on this list.

Source: Mental Floss | Published: 2026-11-27 01:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: The Original 'Meet the Parents' Wasn't the Movie You Remember
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

November 25 sees the release of Focker-In-Law, the newest film in the Meet the Parents franchise. The 2000 installment follows Ben Stiller and his fiancÃ©e, Teri Polo, as he meets her mother and father (played by Blythe Danner and Robert De Niro) for the first time, and the comedic chaos that follows.

However, this movie was not actually an original production: it was a remake of the 1992 indie film of the same title, directed by the filmmaker Greg Glienna. The original is also a much darker film than its more famous remake: as Variety put it, "Who ever heard of a comedy where everyone gets maimed, drowned, shot or commits suicide?... 'Meet the Parents' turns a visit with the in-laws into a living nightmare." Here's a look at the original film on which a long-running franchise was built (and which the distributor later tried to keep the public from seeing).

Inside the Indie That Inspired Meet the Parents

Like the later version of the story, the 1992 film explores the idea of what happens when a man meets his future in-laws, but in Glienna's version, it ventures into much more serious territory, with multiple characters being killed as the story unfolds. Unlike the expensive Hollywood remake, the original was shot on a budget of only $30,000, and in addition to directing, Glienna played the lead role and co-wrote the script with Mary Ruth Clark. The project was originally sold to National Lampoon to be released as part of their self-titled series of films, but the deal fell through, leaving its future uncertain at first. Â

However, it received some positive critical attention when it made its debut: Variety reviewed the film when it premiered at the 1992 Just for Laughs Comedy Festival in Montreal, and described it as a "wonderfully twisted dark comedy." Their review also gives a number of details about the little-seen movie's story, including their summary of the plot's framing device: "Presented almost entirely in flashback, the tale begins when a gas station attendant warns a client en route to meet the future in-laws to 'turn back' while he still can. What follows is the tragic story of a previous future groom who didnât take the advice." The disasters which befall the characters include a saga in which "Greg blinds the mother with a fishing rod, ruins the family car, drowns the dog and accidentally climbs into bed with his fiancÃ©e's sister."

How a Tricky Contract Locked It Away

The original film was not widely distributed, but according to Glienna, one person who did see it was Steven Soderbergh, who liked it so much that he reached out to the writer-director about developing the original into a new version: "He called me and said this should be a big studio film â this is very commercial. And they flew my co-writer, Mary Ruth Clark and myself to New York to work with him for three days, and we worked on the script â his vision of it." Ultimately, Universal acquired the rights to the film with the intention to make a new version based on the same premise.

However, after Glienna sold the remake rights to Universal, it turned out there was a catch in his deal. In a 2024 interview, Glienna explained: "I got a lousy lawyer, and we signed a contract. I don't know why this wasn't explained to me, or I didn't comprehend it, but I could only release it after a certain amount of time in a not-for-profit situation. I don't know why I would have agreed to that. Now, anytime I've tried to get the rights to release the film, they say no. I don't know why they don't want me to release this film."

Glienna expressed his disappointment at the hurdle which had been placed in front of his original version. "We made this film to be seen. Why would they not let us show [it to] people? I don't understand." However, Glienna has attempted to look for the positives in the situation: "I try to look on the bright side. â¦ I'm still getting residuals on something I did 30 years ago." Today, the original film occasionally emerges on YouTube, but it remains to be seen whether it will ever be officially cleared for re-release in the future.

Source: Mental Floss | Published: 2026-11-26 23:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: 20 Co-Stars Who Couldn't Stand Each Other in Real Life
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

In 2001, ABC broadcast an all-star made-for-TV comedy movie called These Old Broads. Co-written by Carrie Fisher, the film told the story of three aging Hollywood starlets whoâdespite hating one anotherâare coaxed into a reunion by their agent, when the film that made their names is rereleased thirty years later.Â

The âold broadsâ in question were played by real-life Hollywood legends Shirley MacLaine, Fisherâs mother Debbie Reynolds, and Joan Collins, while the role of the agent was taken on by Elizabeth Taylor (in her last on-screen performance). The plot, however, was closer to the truth than some viewers might have realized.Â

Behind the scenes, Reynolds and Taylor had long had a bitter falling-out, after Taylor had an affair with Reynoldsâ husband, Eddie Fisher, in the late 1950s. The affair caused a scandal at the timeâmost notably when Fisher went on to marry Taylor just three hours after his and Reynoldsâ divorce was finalized.Â

Happily, by the time These Old Broads came around, the pair had apparently buried the hatchet. But theirs is by no means the only iconic on-screen feud in Hollywood and television history.Â

CLARK GABLE AND VIVIEN LEIGH, GONE WITH THE WIND (1939)

Rumors of an on-set feud between Clark Gable and Vivien Leigh during the making of Gone with the Wind began almost immediately after production started. Itâs certainly true that Vivien Leigh was midway through a long affair with Laurence Olivier during filming, which had led to presumptions that Gable was not too keen on Leighâs infidelity. In return, a persistent rumor claims that Leigh disliked kissing Gable because of his bad breath (allegedly caused by a recurrent gum infection and ill-fitting dentures). How much of this is Hollywood folklore, and how much is rooted in truth, continues to be discussed and debated todayâthough for the record, Gable himself stated categorically in an interview in 1940 that âdespite what a lot of papers said, there was never any feud between Vivien Leigh and me during the filming of Gone with the Wind, or at any time thereafter.âÂ

ERROL FLYNN AND BETTE DAVIS, THE PRIVATE LIVES OF ELIZABETH AND ESSEX (1939)

Bette Davis and legendary Hollywood Lothario Errol Flynn first clashed when they worked together on 1938âs The Sisters, with Davis famously fighting for (and winning) joint billing once she heard that the credits were due to only list Flynnâs name. Their relationship worsened during filming of 1939âs The Private Lives of Elizabeth and Essex, with the duoâs differing acting styles causing considerable tension, and Davis resenting the fact that Flynn was being paid more, despite her rising star power. In rehearsal of a scene in which Davis was to slap Flynn on the face, Flynn recalled later that she âlifted one of her hands, heavy with those Elizabethan rings, and Joe Louis himself couldnât give a right hook better than Bette hooked me.âÂ

SHELLEY WINTERS AND FRANK SINATRA, MEET DANNY WILSON (1952)

At the time of filming 1952âs musical drama Meet Danny Wilson, Frank Sinatra was suffering through something of a career lull, had separated from his first wife Nancy, and was now in an increasingly volatile relationship with his second, Ava Gardner. His personal woes soon began affecting his behavior on setâbut his co-star, the equally feisty and no-nonsense Shelley Winters, was in no mood to tolerate his unprofessionalism. The pair repeatedly clashed throughout filming, with Winters famously labeling Sinatra a âskinny, no-talent stupid Hoboken bastardâ in an explosive row while filming at Burbank Airport.Â

RICHARD WIDMARK AND MARILYN MONROE, DONâT BOTHER TO KNOCK (1952)

âGod-awful to work with. Impossible, really,â was actor Richard Widmarkâs assessment of working with Marilyn Monroe on 1952âs Donât Bother to Knock. Although the pair got along personally, Monroeâs light-hearted style (made worse by her crippling stage fright) clashed with Widmarkâs strictly professional approach to acting, making filming a chore. Widmark, however, understood Monroeâs issues and was largely sympathetic. âIt was all a result of fear,â he later explained. âShe was insecure about so many things and was obviously self-destructive. She was a wounded bird from the beginning.â

ETHEL MERMAN AND MARILYN MONROE, THEREâS NO BUSINESS LIKE SHOWBUSINESS (1954)

Another star who struggled to work alongside Marilyn Monroe was the notoriously plain-speaking Broadway legend Ethel Merman, who worked with her on 1954âs Thereâs No Business Like Showbusiness. Their co-star Mitzi Gaynor later admitted that she ânever saw anybody work so hardâ as Monroe on this movieâbut Merman was less forgiving of Monroeâs nervousness and her tendency to be late to set, famously barking âAll right, whereâs the blond?â when she did not appear on time. Monroe, in return, was reportedly terrified of Mermanâand perhaps wasnât too impressed when her then-husband Joe DiMaggio visited the set, but allegedly requested he only have his photo taken with Merman rather than his wife.Â

HUMPHREY BOGART AND WILLIAM HOLDEN, SABRINA (1954)Â

One of Hollywoodâs longest rumbling feuds was allegedly between Humphrey Bogart and William Holden. The pairâs rocky relationship stemmed from an incident during the filming of Invisible Stripes way back in 1939, in which Holden was due to drive a motorcycle with Bogart in the sidecar. Bogart was unsure of how safe the sidecar was, and refused to do the scene with Holden at the wheel; a stuntman sat in instead, only for the motorcycle to come apart and crash through a brick wall, in Holdenâs words. Bogart, according to Hollywood lore, joked that Holden had tried to kill him.Â…

Lend Your Voice to Freakonomics Radio

We’re working on an episode about behavior change — essentially, how to get yourself to do the things you should be doing but often don’t. It revolves around the fascinating research of Katy Milkman at Penn. For example, she and her colleagues have noted a “Fresh Start Effect”:

The popularity of New Year’s resolutions suggests that people are more likely to tackle their goals immediately following salient temporal landmarks. … We propose that these landmarks demarcate the passage of time, creating many new mental accounting periods each year, which relegate past imperfections to a previous period, induce people to take a big-picture view of their lives, and thus motivate aspirational behaviors.

What we’re looking for are your examples of fresh starts — whether it’s a new timeframe, job, relationship, living situation, etc. — and how it may have motivated some aspirational behaviors of your own.

Many thanks!
